The Kremlin's seeming interest in negotiations aims not to end the war in Ukraine but rather to secure economic concessions from the United States such that Russia can continue funding its war.
Various Russian officials tried to present the October 21 meeting between US Special Representative to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin as evidence that Russia is willing to engage in meaningful negotiations to end the war while simultaneously attempting to extract economic concessions from the United States so that Russia can continue funding the war.[i] Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev, for example, claimed on October 21 that Witkoff and Putin used the October 21 meeting to agree to expand Russian-US economic cooperation and to “continue communicating.”[ii] A Kremlin domestic policy official told Russian opposition source Verstka that the Kremlin does not expect negotiations to resolve the war in Ukraine but that Russian officials hope to extract economic concessions, which could boost Russia’s budget and give Russia a military advantage.[iii]
Other Russian officials meanwhile demonstrated Russia’s unwillingness to make any meaningful concessions toward ending the war in Ukraine.
Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on October 22 that Putin did not present any Russian peace proposal to Witkoff during their meeting and that Putin has not considered the composition of a potential Russian delegation for a future Russia-US-Ukraine trilateral meeting.[iv] Russian State Duma deputies expressed skepticism on October 21 and 22 that negotiations could end the war and reiterated claims that freezing the current frontlines would be detrimental to Russia's own efforts to end the war.[v] A source close to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told Verstka on October 22 that the Kremlin has been working for over 1.5 years to try to sway the Trump administration to Russia's side and that the Kremlin's current negotiation efforts are emphasizing Ukraine's alleged hopelessness.

The Kremlin is fundamentally only interested in buying time to resolve the war on the battlefield while Russia simultaneously reaps the benefits of economic cooperation with the United States.
State Duma Defense Committee First Deputy Chairperson Alexei Zhuravlyov stated on October 21 that Russia must "press" Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the battlefield and force Ukraine to "capitulate."[vii] Zhuravlyov added that Russia should not rely on diplomacy with the United States because Russian "successes on the ground” will strengthen Russia’s negotiating position.[viii] Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov similarly claimed that Russian forces maintain the "complete strategic initiative” and are conducting a "relentless offensive” in all key areas of the frontline.[ix]
Russian forces are not winning on the battlefield, however, particularly as Ukrainian forces have stymied the planned Russian offensive to seize Donetsk Oblast.
ISW has observed evidence that Russian forces suffered a net loss of 241 square kilometers of territory in Ukraine since September 1, 2026.
The average rate of daily Russian advances has significantly declined since 2025, with an average of 0.25 square kilometers per day so far in 2026.
Ukrainian forces have, comparatively, been contesting and seizing the operational initiative across several sectors of the frontline throughout 2026, including most recently in the Lyman direction with Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi which liberated over 270 square kilometers of territory and thwarted the Russian military command’s plan to encircle the Fortress Belt.[x] Russian forces are also facing mounting monthly casualties while the Russian recruitment rate continues to fall short of its loss rate.[xi] Russian forces have suffered almost 37,000 casualties thus far in October 2026 — much higher than the 31,270 casualties for all of October 2025.[xii] The Kremlin may face mounting challenges in the coming months, should Ukraine continue to contest the operational initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans, potentially further pushing Russian commanders to urge Putin to conduct a mobilization in some form.[xiii]

Requests to V4-Pro were set to move to Flash from September 14, and that arrangement runs until a V4.1-Pro arrives.

DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash on Thursday.
It is a smaller model that the company says beats its own flagship on coding and agent tasks, at a lower price.
The Hangzhou lab announced it in a thread on X and published the weights on Hugging Face under the MIT licence.
That lets anyone download, modify and run it.
The launch comes with a notable retirement.
From 04:00 UTC on 14 September, DeepSeek will send every request made to V4-Pro, its top model, to V4.1-Flash instead.
Those requests will be billed at the cheaper Flash rates.
That arrangement runs until a V4.1-Pro arrives.
DeepSeek gave no date for it.
A big model that works like a small one
V4.1-Flash has 552 billion parameters in total.
It uses only a small slice of them for each piece of text.
DeepSeek calls the design a “causal encoder-decoder” and describes it as the smallest model in a new architecture family.
It activates 8 billion parameters per token when reading input and 16 billion when writing output.
That split is aimed at AI agents.
An agent that calls tools repeatedly spends much of its time reading fresh input, so cheaper reading means cheaper agents.
The model handles up to 1 million tokens of context and understands images natively, according to its model card.
DeepSeek says it pre-trained the model on 45 trillion tokens.
The bigger engineering claim concerns memory.
Models keep a cache of what they have already processed, known as the KV cache.
It saves them recomputing everything at every step.
For long agent sessions, that cache eats expensive high-bandwidth memory.
DeepSeek says V4.1-Flash needs 890 bytes per token for it.
That is about a quarter of what V4-Flash needed, and roughly 437 times less than its first model in 2023.
Where it wins, and where it does not
DeepSeek’s own benchmark table puts V4.1-Flash level with the best closed models on some coding tests.
On DeepSWE v1.1, a software engineering benchmark, it scores 74.2.
Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 scores 74.0 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol 73.0.
On CyberGym, a cybersecurity test, it scores 88.1, ahead of every rival with a listed score.
The same table shows clear gaps.
On Humanity’s Last Exam, a hard academic test, it scores 36.8 to Opus 5’s 56.3.
On ProgramBench it reaches 20.3 against 37.0 for Opus 5.
On Terminal-Bench 3.0 it trails both US models.
These are DeepSeek’s figures.
TNW has not independently verified them.
Its closest Chinese rival looks weaker by DeepSeek’s count.
The table puts V4.1-Flash ahead of Moonshot’s Kimi K3 on every agent and coding test where both have scores.
Kimi K3 still leads on GPQA Diamond and Humanity’s Last Exam.
In August, TNW covered an experimental multimodal model that DeepSeek pitched against Anthropic.
V4.1-Flash replaces it.
The Decoder’s Jonathan Kemper, who read the technical report, flagged a less flattering part of it.
DeepSeek describes reward hacking during training, with agents occasionally using newly published vulnerabilities or wiping important system files in their test environments.
It also admits the model lags the best closed systems at reading complicated images.
A price cut, a month after a price rise
DeepSeek says the cheaper architecture lets it serve more users at lower cost.
It says it is “passing the savings on” to customers.
The new rates took effect at 04:00 UTC on Thursday.
Off-peak, one million tokens of output cost $0.60, and cached input costs $0.003.
Peak rates, which apply on weekday mornings UTC, are double.
Bloomberg Intelligence analysts put the cut at as much as 32%.
The move reverses the direction of travel from August, when DeepSeek launched a Claude Code rival and quadrupled its prices.
Customers still on V4-Pro will now pay Flash rates for what DeepSeek says is a better model.
Cheap Chinese models have squeezed rivals for months, in what analysts have called a ‘death zone’ for US model makers.
In early August, TNW reported that V4-Flash was already the cheapest well-known model to run.
Rivals and investors react
The pressure landed on Chinese competitors first.
Shares in MiniMax and Z.ai fell more than 8% in Hong Kong on Thursday.
Alibaba slid more than 2%, Bloomberg’s Saritha Rai reported.
The timing matters for DeepSeek’s own plans.
Reuters reported that the company has begun preparing for a listing on Shanghai’s STAR Market.
That follows the IPO preparations TNW covered in July.
DeepSeek is also courting operators directly.
It says it will work with the open-source community on inference support, and invited anyone planning a deployment of 2,000 GPUs with a storage cluster to get in touch.
Coding tools WorkBuddy and OpenCode already support the model.
The open question is whether DeepSeek’s benchmarks hold up in independent testing, and what V4.1-Pro costs when it arrives.
Until then, every V4-Pro customer becomes a V4.1-Flash customer on Monday.

DeepSeek V4.1 Pro 什么时候发布？官方已确认在开发中，时间待定
DeepSeek V4.1 Pro 是 DeepSeek 正在开发中的下一代旗舰模型。关于发布时间，核心结论是：DeepSeek 官方已确认其存在，但尚未公布任何具体的发布日期、参数规模或技术细节。 它目前仍处于开发阶段，上线时间待定。
一、官方如何确认 V4.1 Pro 的存在
2026 年 9 月 9 日，DeepSeek 技术团队成员崔天翼（@tianyi）在 X 平台发布通知：一旦 V4.1 Flash 正式上线，所有指向 DeepSeek V4 Pro 的 API 请求将被路由至 V4.1 Flash 并按 Flash 费率计费，“这一安排将持续到 DeepSeek V4.1 Pro 本身上线为止”。
这句话中的“直到 V4.1 Pro 上线为止”，是 DeepSeek 官方首次在内部沟通中明确承认这款旗舰产品的存在。随后，多家中国媒体对此进行了报道和佐证。
二、当前状态：没有任何技术细节公布
截至 2026 年 9 月 11 日，关于 DeepSeek V4.1 Pro 的信息极为有限：
- 没有发布日期：官方未给出任何时间窗口或路线图
- 没有技术报告：没有参数规模、架构设计、训练数据等任何技术文档
- 没有模型卡：在 Hugging Face 或 DeepSeek 开放平台上均无模型页面
- 无法调用：没有任何 API 端点响应 deepseek-v4.1-pro 这个名称
目前所有关于 V4.1 Pro 的信息，都建立在一条团队成员的社交帖子及其被媒体引用的基础之上。“架构已解决”等说法属于外部观察者的推断，并非官方确认。
三、为什么 V4.1 Pro 尚未发布
资源调配是主要原因之一。DeepSeek 将 V4 Pro 的请求路由至 V4.1 Flash 后，可以释放出原本用于服务 V4 Pro 的算力资源，用于 V4.1 Pro 的研发。V4 Pro 本身是一个 1.6 万亿参数的旗舰模型，其下线释放的 GPU 资源相当可观。
V4.1 Flash 的“越级”表现也给了 DeepSeek 喘息空间。官方称 V4.1 Flash 在性能、成本、速度和总用时上全面超越 V4 Pro，这意味着在 V4.1 Pro 就绪之前，用户仍能获得比前代旗舰更好的服务。
四、如何获取最新进展
由于 V4.1 Pro 尚未发布，建议关注以下渠道获取第一手信息：
- DeepSeek 开放平台（platform.deepseek.com ）：新模型上线时通常会在此更新 API 文档和定价页面
- DeepSeek 官方公众号/官网：V4 Pro 正式版发布时，官方通过公众号进行了公告
- DeepSeek 技术团队成员社交账号：V4.1 Pro 的存在最初就是通过团队成员的社交帖

TL;DR
DeepSeek V4.1 Pro is a referenced future successor to V4 Pro, with no release date established by the official sources reviewed on October 14, 2026.
The September 10 Flash announcement provides the clearest release clue.
Available Flash specifications and evaluations help developers prepare, but they do not establish Pro capabilities.
DeepSeek has clarified that V4 Pro remains available in response to user demand.
Benchmark figures below describe the original Flash release, not the October 17 Flash-1017 update; integrations should verify provider-specific model versions before deployment.
Key Takeaways
- Release status: V4.1 Pro has been referenced officially, but no specific launch date is confirmed.
- Most important clue: The V4.1 Flash announcement connected a future V4.1 Pro to an API transition plan.
- API status: DeepSeek confirmed continued V4 Pro service with unchanged billing in response to user demand; the earlier plan to redirect Pro requests to Flash is superseded.
- Technical foundation: V4.1 Flash discloses a 552B-parameter backbone, asymmetric processing and a 1M-token context.
- Preparation: Benchmark existing models and keep API model identifiers configurable.
When Will DeepSeek V4.1 Pro Be Released?
As of October 14, 2026, the official sources reviewed for this article do not establish a release date for DeepSeek V4.1 Pro.
Its name appears in DeepSeek’s product communication, but a future-product reference is not a launch schedule.
On September 10, 2026, DeepSeek introduced V4.1 Flash as the smallest member of a new architecture family.
Its official launch announcement described an initial plan to redirect the older V4 Pro API to V4.1 Flash until the future V4.1 Pro release.
The statement ties the successor to a concrete migration policy, but does not establish a launch date, training status or final specifications.
DeepSeek V4.1 Pro Release Timeline
| Date | Development | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| April 24, 2026 | V4 preview family released | Previous generation baseline |
| August 13, 2026 | V4 Pro general-availability update | Known flagship baseline |
| September 10, 2026 | V4.1 Flash announced; V4.1 Pro referenced | New architecture family introduced, with a future Pro successor referenced but no release date confirmed |
| September 14, 2026 | Original V4 Pro migration target | Subsequently revised |
| V4.1 Pro release | No announced date | Timing remains unconfirmed |
The official news archive dates the V4 preview release to April 24 and the V4 Pro general release to August 13.
The September migration date was a service-transition target, not a V4.1 Pro release date.
The September announcement proposed redirecting V4 Pro requests to Flash from September 14 until a future Pro release.
However, the current API documentation lists V4 Pro as a separate model with its own rates.
DeepSeek subsequently clarified in its official September 10 changelog entry that it would continue providing V4 Pro API service after September 14 in response to user demand, with billing unchanged.
The earlier redirection proposal should therefore be treated as a superseded plan, not the current V4 Pro routing policy.
The current model table lists deepseek-v4-pro as V4-Pro-0813 and deepseek-flash as V4.1-Flash-1017; verify each provider’s model mapping before deployment.
Future confirmation should come from a dedicated DeepSeek announcement, a supported API identifier, and published Pro evaluations and pricing.
What Has DeepSeek Officially Confirmed About V4.1 Pro?
Confirmed Information
The distinction between official statements and technical speculation is essential before launch.
V4.1 Flash disclosures provide substantial evidence about the architecture family, but do not automatically become V4.1 Pro specifications.
DeepSeek has referenced V4.1 Pro as a future member of the V4.1 family, but the sources reviewed do not establish its release date, public model identifier, parameter count, context window, vision support, reasoning controls, benchmark results or API pricing.
The available V4.1 Flash specifications provide context for the architecture family, not confirmed V4.1 Pro specifications.
DeepSeek describes V4.1 Flash as the smallest member of a new family designed for scaling.
This supports a larger future architecture but does not prove V4.1 Pro will simply be a bigger copy.
Training, active parameter budgets, attention schemes and post-training methods remain unconfirmed.
Community Reports / Leaks
In a September 27, 2026 X post, @NFT_Chen claimed that DeepSeek V4.1 Pro had appeared in internal testing with account-gated early access.
@NFT_Chen’s post is an unverified community report, not an official DeepSeek announcement.
The screenshot visibly shows the V4.1 Pro name, an early-access label and several configuration fields, but it does not establish the screenshot’s source, deployment environment, connection to a live model, public API availability or final product specifications.
Treat it as a lead for further verification rather than as evidence of a confirmed release.
The attached configuration screenshot displays the name DeepSeek V4.1 Pro, an Early access tagline, high reasoning effort, and flags for training data use, non-premium access and no multimodal support.
It also contains a FREEBUFF_AI_TRAINING_NOTICE identifier.
If authentic and tied to an active integration, the entry could be an early-access clue.
An availability flag is not a service guarantee, and the near-launch prediction by the author is not a confirmed release window.
Treat the screenshot as a lead for further verification, not as a Pro specification.
What Is Known About DeepSeek V4.1 Pro?
V4.1 Flash offers the clearest technical foundation for the upcoming family.
V4.1 Flash uses a Causal Encoder-Decoder architecture with different computation paths for prefill and decoding.
According to the technical model card, the released model contains 40 Transformer layers across a 20-layer encoder and 20-layer decoder.
| Specification | DeepSeek V4 Pro | V4.1 Flash | V4.1 Pro |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backbone parameters | 1.6T | 552B | Unannounced |
| Activated parameters | 49B | 8B input / 16B output | Unannounced |
| Architecture | MoE | Causal Encoder-Decoder MoE | Unannounced |
| Context window | 1M | 1M | Unannounced |
| Max output | 384K | 384K | Unannounced |
| Native image input | Not in listed configuration | Supported | Unannounced |
| KV cache footprint | Not directly comparable | ~890 bytes/token | Unannounced |
| Reasoning control | Low / high / max | Continuous 1–100 | Unannounced |
| Availability | API | API and open weights | Not announced |
Although V4.1 Flash contains 552B backbone parameters, only about 8B parameters are activated per input token and 16B during output.
Causal Encoder-Decoder Scaling Potential
The separation between prefill and decoding may make it possible for future family members to increase representation capacity while managing inference costs.
V4.1 Flash also features Compressed Sparse Attention 2 and FP4 KV caching.
Whether and how V4.1 Pro inherits these characteristics remains unknown.
DeepSeek reports a global KV-cache footprint of approximately 890 bytes per token for V4.1 Flash, compared with 3,514 bytes for V4 Flash.
This is a global KV-cache comparison, not a measure of total serving memory.
The two original graphics reproduced in this article are published in DeepSeek’s official model card; neither graphic is a V4.1 Pro result.
DeepSeek V4.1 Pro vs V4 Pro vs V4.1 Flash
A useful starting point is the observed difference between existing models, not an invented Pro benchmark.

Google may be back at the frontier of artificial intelligence, but investors and consumers are increasingly focusing on what people can build with the technology as personal agents surge in popularity.
The company unveiled its long-awaited Gemini 4 Argon model on Wednesday, promising major advances in coding, cybersecurity, and complex tasks.
According to industry benchmarks, Argon ties OpenAI on a key cybersecurity test and posts leading results in software engineering.
Argon's introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens also matches OpenAI's newly discounted GPT-6.1 Sol model.
A token is equivalent to about three-quarters of one word.
While Google is stepping up its game in the model battle, rival Meta is racking up millions of downloads for its Muse app, which launched last month and soared to the top of Apple's App Store, topping ChatGPT.
Earlier this week, OpenAI rolled out Dots, its personal agent offering, capitalizing on demand from businesses and consumers for tools that can carry out tasks — like scouring emails, booking travel and organizing expenses — on a user's behalf.
Meanwhile, the attention at the frontier model level has turned to safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei sparking a firestorm three weeks ago by urging the top AI labs to slow the pace of development as concerns intensify about their potential dangers.
Over the past three months, Alphabet's stock is down about 6%, while Meta is up 19% over that stretch, sparked by September's rally, which was the sharpest for any month since 2022.
Analysts at JPMorgan Chase wrote in a note on Thursday that Google needs a significant advance in its personal agent offerings to generate consumer enthusiasm.
Bank of America identified the potential for Gemini 4 to strengthen Google's cloud business and existing products, while providing a foundation for a future personal agent.
In the consumer market, Google has a massive home-court advantage.
Billions of people use Google products, including Gmail, Calendar, Chrome, and Search.
Their messages and schedules are already stored within Google's ecosystem, potentially giving the company a substantial edge in developing an assistant capable of working across those services.
Yet Google's personal agent, Spark, remains limited to paying subscribers, while Muse is free with usage caps.
As of Sept.
30, Muse had reached more than 5 million downloads, according to Sensor Tower.
In a background briefing with CNBC, members of Google's agent team outlined Spark's existing capabilities and the company's approach to expanding access, and acknowledged that Muse's free availability has helped consumers discover and experiment with it.
Launched in May at Google's I/O developers conference, Spark can work across Gmail and Calendar, navigate websites through Chrome, and complete tasks such as filling out online forms.
It's also available through Google's mobile and desktop apps.
But unlike Muse, Spark can't make outbound phone calls or complete purchases on a user's behalf.
Instead, it takes users through the purchasing process before handing control back to them for final approval.
Can Argon help Spark?
Meta's approach has also introduced complications.
Reuters reported in September that the company had experimented with a human concierge system in which contractors handled some phone calls when Muse couldn't complete them autonomously.
Internal privacy concerns prompted Meta to suspend the experiment, while its automated phone-calling feature remains in beta.
The episode has raised privacy concerns associated with granting AI assistants access to so much sensitive personal information.
A Meta spokesperson said in an email that internal testing "is core to the product development process" and is being done to get feedback on safety and privacy protections needed for a broader release.
"We're working with merchants to continue improving this potential calling feature, and will only roll it out when it's ready and with the proper disclosures," the spokesperson said.
Google is now evaluating whether its latest frontier model could strengthen Spark.
In an interview with CNBC, Tulsee Doshi, head of product for Gemini, highlighted Argon's ability to tackle complicated assignments that require multiple steps and can run for extended periods.
She said Google is still evaluating where Argon can be deployed most effectively.
Personal agents don't need the most powerful frontier models to complete everyday tasks.
And prior to Argon, Google spent much of the summer releasing cheaper, lighter models designed to handle routine requests at scale.
Doshi said those models remain essential for everyday agents, while more powerful frontier models can provide the additional reasoning capabilities required for complex assignments.
There's also the money.
Running powerful AI models is expensive, particularly for agents that operate continuously and perform multiple tasks.
Google's introductory Argon pricing is competitive, but the company said its published rates will eventually double to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.
One challenge for Google is determining how to combine its models into an agent that can handle increasingly sophisticated tasks without making the service prohibitively expensive to operate.
Argon also isn't broadly available yet.
Google is participating in a voluntary U.S.
government safety-testing process and initially restricting access to select cybersecurity defenders and enterprise cloud customers.
The company plans to expand availability to developers, enterprise customers and consumers, but hasn't announced a public release date.
That's limiting the independent testing of Argon's capabilities.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that some Google employees had questioned the model's real-world coding performance despite strong benchmark results.
Google disputes that characterization, and told CNBC that employees across the company have been testing versions of Gemini 4 for weeks, with some receiving unlimited access.
But the greater urgency is on the agent side, as other companies race to bring AI to the masses.
As JPMorgan analysts wrote, "Google has struggled to translate ongoing product velocity into splashy releases that resonate with consumers, capture sustained mindshare, & meaningfully drive sentiment around AI leadership."
—CNBC's Jonathan Vanian contributed to this report.

Crude Oil Near $100, Brent–WTI Spread Widens on War and Inventory Draws

WTI nears $100 and Brent above $110 amid Iran war, tanker attacks and U.S.
stock draws.
Backwardation steepens and diesel cracks stay firm, supporting prices.
Prices & Curve Structure
NYMEX WTI futures show a very steep backwardation from December 2026 at 99.08 USD/bbl to mid‑2030s contracts around the low‑50s USD/bbl, with the Dec 26–Dec 27 spread at roughly 18 USD/bbl.
The first few contracts recorded strong daily gains on 22 October, with Dec 26 up 1.93 USD/bbl (+1.95%) and Jan 27 up 2.06 USD/bbl (+2.11%), highlighting concentrated strength at the front end of the curve.
ICE Brent mirrors this structure at a higher absolute level: Dec 26 settled at 113.05 USD/bbl, gaining 4.23 USD/bbl (+3.74%) on the day, while Dec 27 trades around 86.56 USD/bbl and longer‑dated 2030–2032 maturities slip into the low‑70s and high‑60s USD/bbl area.
The Brent–WTI spread is currently around 13–14 USD/bbl, with independent quotes putting Brent at 112.66 USD/bbl and WTI at 99.54–99.47 USD/bbl on 22 October, and a spread future near -13.7 USD/bbl (WTI minus Brent).
Refined products are amplifying the move: front‑month ICE low‑sulfur gasoil (diesel) stands at 1477.50 USD/t for November 2026, up 46.00 USD/t (+3.11%) on the day, with a similarly backwardated structure out through 2032.
Diesel cracks, although off their peak, remain historically elevated according to the latest IEA oil market update, sustaining strong refinery margins for middle distillates even as crude feedstock becomes more expensive.
Supply, Demand & Geopolitics
On the supply side, the key driver is the Iran war and escalating disruption risk through the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest reports confirm that seven oil tankers were damaged or set on fire in the area overnight, the highest tempo of attacks since the early weeks of the conflict, stoking fears of a broader closure or self‑sanctioning by shipowners.
Despite attacks, crude exports via Hormuz have so far held above pre‑war levels on a rolling basis thanks to workarounds such as ship‑to‑ship transfers off the UAE coast.
Still, the cost of moving each barrel has risen sharply, feeding directly into delivered prices and contributing to the growing seaborne premium embedded in Brent.
Global fundamentals remain tight.
OPEC’s latest outlook points to demand rising from 105.7 million b/d in 2026 to 108.3 million b/d in 2027, implying another robust year of consumption growth layered on top of already strained logistics and moderate non‑OPEC supply additions.
The IEA highlights counter‑seasonal draws in OECD gasoil stocks to multi‑year lows, underlining that refined product inventories, not just crude, are anchoring strength in the complex.
Inventories & Fundamentals
In the U.S., the latest Weekly Petroleum Status Report for the week ending 16 October shows commercial crude stocks falling by 3.1 million barrels to around 412.5 million barrels, roughly 10 million barrels below last year and slightly under the five‑year average.
This reinforces the signal from the futures curve that prompt physical availability is tightening even in inland hubs, despite high outright prices.
Globally, crude and product stocks continue to trend below pre‑conflict norms.
Earlier this quarter, EIA data still showed total crude plus product inventories in the OECD hovering near the bottom of their 2021–2025 range, while the IEA notes OECD gasoil stocks in July were 5% below pre‑war levels and at their lowest since late 2023.
Low stocks, alongside persistent demand, limit the system’s shock‑absorption capacity and magnify the price impact of every new disruption headline.
Freight, Diesel & Macro Links
Freight markets are a key transmission channel from geopolitics to fundamentals.
The IEA underscores that surging crude tanker rates in September sharply lifted delivered crude costs and compressed refining margins, especially in Europe, where diesel cracks fell from around 100 USD/bbl to near 60 USD/bbl by early October.
However, with Hormuz risk premiums and war‑related insurance surcharges rising again, freight costs are back under upward pressure, with likely renewed pass‑through into diesel and jet prices in the coming weeks.
Downstream, consumers are increasingly feeling the squeeze.
Brent has risen more than 70% since the start of 2026, with prices moving from the low‑70s in early March to above 109 USD/bbl in October, translating into sharply higher gasoline and home‑heating oil bills.
This feeds into broader inflation, as reflected in higher food and logistics costs noted by recent macro analyses, and keeps central banks cautious even as growth headwinds emerge.
Short‑Term Outlook & Trading Views
Over the next few sessions, market direction will hinge on three interlocking factors: (1) the intensity and geographic spread of tanker attacks in and around Hormuz; (2) weekly inventory signals from the U.S.
EIA, particularly at Cushing and the Gulf Coast; and (3) any incremental policy moves from OPEC+ and key consuming countries, such as SPR releases or new sanctions.
Trading outlook (1–3 week horizon)
- Bias: Price risks remain skewed to the upside as long as Hormuz shipping attacks continue and U.S.
crude and gasoil inventories trend sideways to lower.
- Curve trades: The pronounced backwardation (WTI Dec 26 near 99 USD/bbl vs.
mid‑2030s in the low‑50s) offers attractive roll yield for length in the front third of the curve; however, volatility and margin requirements are elevated.
- Brent–WTI spread: With the spread near 13–14 USD/bbl and coastal logistics under strain, further widening is possible if inland U.S.
stocks rebuild while seaborne availability tightens; conversely, any de‑escalation in Hormuz would likely compress the spread.
- Products: ICE gasoil’s stronger percentage gains vs.
crude, coupled with low OECD gasoil stocks, support maintaining constructive exposure to middle‑distillate cracks, particularly into Northern Hemisphere winter.

GOP Could Flip Michigan Senate Seat for First Time in Nearly 50 Years

Republicans have a shot at a Michigan Senate seat that Democrats have held since 1979, and three weeks before Election Day on November 3 the race between former Representative Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is close.
The seat is open because Democratic Senator Gary Peters decided not to seek a third term.
Democrats have held it since Carl Levin defeated Republican Senator Robert Griffin in 1978.
Levin served for 36 years before Peters succeeded him in 2015.
A Rogers victory would also end a longer losing streak for Republicans.
The party has not won a Senate race in Michigan since 1994, when Spencer Abraham captured the state's other seat in the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed holds a slight lead in polls released this month, mostly within the margin of error.
The Cook Political Report rates the race a Toss-Up, and strategists in both parties count it among the handful of contests likely to determine who controls the chamber in January.
Rogers came within 20,000 votes of beating now-Senator Elissa Slotkin in 2024.
He had no primary opponent this time and carries President Donald Trump's endorsement.
El-Sayed, a progressive and former public health official backed by independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, edged Michigan Representative Haley Stevens in the August 4 Democratic primary by less than a percentage point.
Newsweek reached out to the Rogers and El-Sayed campaigns for comment via email on Monday.
Mike Rogers vs.
Abdul El-Sayed: Latest Polls
Six polls taken between late September and this past weekend have El-Sayed ahead, from 1 point to 7 percentage points.
The newest, an InsiderAdvantage survey of 1,200 likely voters conducted October 9-10, put El-Sayed at 48 percent and Rogers at 46 percent, with 5 percent undecided.
Other recent surveys showed a race inside the margin of error.
Quantus Insights found El-Sayed up 48 percent to 47 percent among 744 likely voters polled October 5-6.
YouGov, working with a much larger sample of 3,947 likely voters September 22-October 4, also landed on a one-point gap, 49 percent to 48 percent.
Mitchell Research & Communications polled 682 likely voters on October 1 and had El-Sayed at 46 percent to Rogers' 41 percent, with third-party candidates splitting about 7 percent and 6 percent unsure.
El-Sayed's biggest lead, 49 percent to 42 percent, came from Z to A Research in a poll sponsored by Rust Belt Rising, a Democratic group.
Summer looked different.
A poll taken a week before the primary for the Michigan Education Association and Business Leaders for Michigan had Rogers up 48 percent to 41 percent over El-Sayed among voters certain to cast a ballot, while Stevens led Rogers by 2.
Independents broke for Rogers over El-Sayed 47 percent to 19 percent in that survey.
Democrats Have Held Michigan Senate Seat Since 1979
At the presidential level, Michigan bounces around.
It went for Trump in 2016 and 2024 and for Joe Biden in 2020.
Senate races have been another story, with Democrats winning every one for nearly three decades.
Rogers nearly broke that run two years ago in his loss to Slotkin.
Republicans took the result as proof he could win, and Trump, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, and the national party got behind him early, clearing the field.
The Democratic primary handed the GOP a second opening.
Stevens had much of the party establishment on her side, Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer among them, and El-Sayed's win left a split coalition.
Some members of the state's Jewish community have voiced concern over his past remarks on Israel.
National Republicans went straight at it.
An ad from the National Republican Senatorial Committee calls El-Sayed the most radical candidate in the country, and the committee has taken to using his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.
In a statement released with the ad, South Carolina Senator Tim Scott, who chairs the committee, said El-Sayed's record makes him "dangerous and ultimately disqualified from serving."
Trump weighed in on October 7, the night before the candidates' first debate, calling El-Sayed "Mohammed" in a Truth Social post and writing that he "goes back to the days of the Jihad."
"He's not just attacking me.
He's attacking all of us," El-Sayed wrote back.
Born in the U.S.
to Egyptian immigrant parents, he also noted that the president clearly knows his name, since he says it every day.
Sanders jumped in on X.
With healthcare, groceries, housing and childcare out of reach for so many families, he wrote that "the best they can do is attack Abdul's Muslim faith."
Rogers has spent the past few weeks stepping away from the White House on a couple of big issues.
In September, he said the war with Iran (which is now 7 1/2 months old) had to "end quickly." Then, on October 7, his campaign put out an ad going after Trump's tariffs on Canada.
"Canada is not our enemy," Rogers said in it.
El-Sayed keeps tying Rogers to Trump, hammering him on prices, housing costs and what the administration's trade fights have done to Michigan's economy.
Latest Developments in Michigan Senate Race
Rogers and El-Sayed debated for the first time on October 8, at WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids.
It got personal fast.
The two talked over each other for much of the hour and kept going during a commercial break.
"In 30 years of doing debates, I've never seen it continue during the commercial," moderator Rick Albin said.
On Iran and Canada, Rogers held his ground.
After the debate, he told reporters that he had called the White House that week to push for a deal on the tariffs.
He went further on immigration, saying the administration's enforcement surge in Minnesota earlier this year, when two protesters were shot and killed, "were probably not appropriate."
Much of the questioning aimed at El-Sayed was about Israel.
Would he back sending weapons if another country attacked it?
He answered that he did not want U.S.
tax dollars going "to subsidize war abroad." A follow-up asked whether Iran or Israel was the bigger threat, and he dismissed it as a "ridiculous question," adding that both had proven dangerous in their own way.
Reporters also pressed him afterward on his ties to Hasan Piker, a streamer with a record of inflammatory comments.
Comparing the most powerful man in the world to a streamer in California, El-Sayed said, was "silly."
As his poll numbers have slipped, Rogers has gotten sharper, too.
Speaking to conservative commentator Ben Shapiro, he called El-Sayed "the most anti-American candidate in the race, in the country."
Money is on Rogers' side.
El-Sayed has been outspent close to 2-to-1 on ads, the Associated Press reported, and is trying to make up for it with a packed travel schedule and interviews everywhere from Fox News to The New York Times.
Rogers has kept a lighter public calendar while outside groups pour money into the state for him.
Democratic leaders are starting to close ranks.
Whitmer campaigned with El-Sayed on debate day, her first appearance with him since backing Stevens in the primary, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York will join the campaign this week.
Former President Barack Obama is expected to rally in Detroit with El-Sayed and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, on Saturday.
A second debate is expected before the end of the month.
Why Is Michigan Race Important in 2026 Midterms?
Republicans control the Senate 53-47.
Vice President JD Vance breaks ties, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take over.
The party has targets.
Cook rates Republican-held seats in Maine and Ohio as Toss-Ups and North Carolina as Lean Democratic, and Democrats are also spending in Alaska and Texas.
Michigan is where that math gets harder.
It is the most vulnerable seat Democrats are defending this cycle, and losing it would require flipping five Republican seats instead of four.
